# **4. Core Business Logic**

Business logic is the part of the program that makes decisions and calculations about the product itself, as opposed to drawing screens or moving data. For CampusNotes the main calculations are the learner's progress through a course, the administrator's totals, and later the quiz score. This section states what the screenshots already prove and what still has to be shown.

## **4.1 Course Progress Calculation**

The course reader shows "Progress: 0 of 21 modules" with a progress bar in the top right corner (Figure 5). This is the first business calculation of the product: how much of a course a student has completed. The formula follows from the Week 4 design, where progress_modules records the completed modules of a student:

**Formula**

**Progress (%) = completed modules ÷ total modules in the course × 100.** The total comes from the number of rows in modules for the course (21 for SE-01). The completed count comes from the rows in progress_modules for the student and that course.

The table gives the expected results for the course in Figure 5 (21 modules). It is also the test table: the interface must show exactly these values.

| **Completed modules** | **Text on screen** | **Progress bar** | **Note** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Progress: 0 of 21 modules | 0% | Observed in Figure 5. |
| 1 | Progress: 1 of 21 modules | 4.8% | Each module is worth 100 ÷ 21 = 4.76%. |
| 7 | Progress: 7 of 21 modules | 33.3% | One third of the course. |
| 10 | Progress: 10 of 21 modules | 47.6% |  |
| 14 | Progress: 14 of 21 modules | 66.7% | Two thirds of the course. |
| 21 | Progress: 21 of 21 modules | 100% | Course complete. |

- **Edge cases to handle:** a course with 0 modules must show 0% instead of dividing by zero; a module that is deleted after being completed must not push the result above 100%; the bar must never exceed 100%.

- **Rounding:** show the text as whole numbers (n of N) and round the bar to one decimal, so the numbers never contradict each other.

- **Where the calculation lives:** in one small function used by every screen, not repeated inside page components, so that a single change and a single set of tests covers it.

**To verify**

The screenshots show the result for 0 completed modules only. Mark one module as completed (or add that action if it does not exist yet) and capture the indicator after the change, then reload the page and confirm the value is kept.

## **4.6 Recommendation: One Domain Module**

**Keep the calculations out of the screens**

Put the progress and quiz-score calculations, with the business rules above, in one place (for example a lib/domain folder) as small functions that take plain numbers and return plain results. Then each page only displays the result. The same functions are used by the server routes, and a handful of tests can prove the examples in this section automatically. This also gives the supervisor a clear "core engine" to point at.

# **5. Server-Side Input Validation and Error Handling**

Anything that comes from a browser can be wrong or hostile. A form check in the page helps the user, but an attacker can skip the page and call the server directly. The rule is therefore: **the server validates everything again and decides.**

## **5.1 What Exists on the Server**

| **Item (evidence)** | **Purpose** | **What is not visible** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| app/api/auth/login/route.ts (Figures 1 and 2, new) | Server endpoint for signing in. | The input checks and the error answers. |
| app/api/notes/route.ts (Figures 1 and 2, new) | Server endpoint for notes data. | Which actions it supports and how it checks input. |
| app/auth/callback (Figures 1 and 2) | Receives the redirect after authentication or e-mail confirmation. | Its content. |
| lib/supabaseAdmin (Figure 2, new) | A database client for server code only. | That it uses a server-side key and is never imported by a page. |
| @supabase/ssr import (Figure 1) | Supabase helper for Next.js that keeps the session consistent between browser and server. | The cookie settings. |

**Check the key rule**

A server-side client may use a powerful key, so the file must never be imported by a browser component, and the key must not start with NEXT_PUBLIC_. Confirm both, because a key in browser code is visible to every visitor.

## **5.2 Defence in Layers**

Good systems check the same input at several levels, so one missing check does not cause damage.

| **Layer** | **Job** | **Example for CampusNotes** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Browser form | Help the user quickly. Never trusted. | The Add New Course form shows examples "e.g. CS-301" and "e.g. Operating Systems" (Figure 4); required fields; the category list. |
| 2. Server route | The real check: type, length, format, allowed values. | Course code present and short, title present, category one of the allowed values, ids are valid UUIDs. |
| 3. Business rules | Check that the action is allowed. | Only an administrator may create or delete courses; a duplicate code is refused. |
| 4. Database | Last line of defence: types, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, foreign keys, CHECK. | Unique course code, module.course_id must exist (Week 4 schema). |

## **5.3 Validation Rules to Demonstrate**

| **Input** | **Rule** | **Expected answer when broken** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Course code | Required, trimmed, 2 to 20 characters, unique | 422 with the field name; 409 for a duplicate |
| Course title | Required, 1 to 200 characters | 422 with the field name |
| Category | Required, one of the allowed categories | 422 |
| Course id in the address (/course/<id>) | Must be a valid UUID that exists | A friendly "course not found" page, not a crash |
| Login e-mail and password | E-mail format; password not empty | 401 with one generic message for every failure |
| JSON body | Valid JSON of the expected shape | 400 for broken JSON |
| Any request to an administrator action without a session or as a student | Session and role required | 401 or 403 |

## **5.4 Error Response Standard**

All errors use the format defined in Week 4, so the screens can handle them in one way: an object with an error that holds a stable **code**, a short human **message** and, for validation, a list of **details** naming each wrong field. The status code tells the class of problem.

| **HTTP** | **Code** | **When** | **Message shown to the user** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | BAD_REQUEST | Broken JSON | "The request could not be read." |
| 401 | UNAUTHENTICATED / INVALID_CREDENTIALS | No session; wrong e-mail or password | "Please sign in." / "Incorrect e-mail or password." |
| 403 | FORBIDDEN | Signed in but not allowed | "You are not allowed to do this." |
| 404 | NOT_FOUND | Course, module or note does not exist | "Not found." |
| 409 | CONFLICT | Duplicate course code | "A course with this code already exists." |
| 422 | VALIDATION_ERROR | A field failed validation | Message under the wrong field |
| 500 | INTERNAL_ERROR | Unexpected failure | "Something went wrong. Please try again." |

- **Never leak internals.** Database messages, table names and stack traces go to the server log, not to the browser.

- **One generic login message.** The same text for "unknown e-mail" and "wrong password", so an attacker cannot learn which e-mails exist.

- **Show errors, do not hide them.** A failed request must show a visible message on the page and leave the form usable.

- **Log on the server.** Every 500 error is written to the server log with enough detail to repair it.

## **5.5 Verification Checklist for Each Route**

| **Check** | **How to test** | **Pass when** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Missing fields | Submit the form or call the route with empty values | 422 and a message naming the field |
| Wrong types and extra long text | Very long title; text where a number is expected | 422, not a server crash |
| Hostile text | Enter <script>alert(1)</script> as a title | Stored or refused safely and shown as plain text |
| Wrong method | Open a POST-only route in the browser address bar | 405 or a clear JSON error |
| No session | Call an administrator action while signed out | 401 |
| Wrong role | Call an administrator action as a student | 403 |
| Database failure | Temporarily use a wrong URL or key | 500 with a generic message; no internal detail on screen |

# **6. The Vertical Slice**

A vertical slice is one complete feature cut through every layer of the system: the screen the user touches, the server that handles the request and the database that stores the data. It proves that the layers fit together, which is more valuable than building one layer fully and leaving the others empty. Week 6 delivers two connected slices, shown in the order the data travels.

| **Slice** | **User story** | **Layers involved** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A. Manage courses | As an administrator I see all courses and can add or delete one. | Admin screens, Supabase client and server routes, courses table |
| B. Read a course | As a student I open a course, see its modules in order and read a module with formatted text. | Course reader, Supabase browser client, courses and modules tables |

## **6.1 Layer Map**

| **Layer** | **What implements it** | **Evidence** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frontend UI | Pages /admin and /course/[id] built with React, Tailwind CSS, lucide icons and react-markdown | Figures 2, 4, 5 |
| Data access from the browser | createBrowserClient from @supabase/ssr in the course page | Figure 1 |
| Backend / API | Next.js server routes api/auth/login and api/notes, plus the authentication callback; a server-side client in lib/supabaseAdmin | Figures 1, 2 |
| Database | Supabase PostgreSQL tables courses and modules with real rows | Figures 3, 4, 5 |

**How the reader gets its data**

The first lines of the course page show that it reads through the Supabase browser client (Figure 1). That path is safe only when Row Level Security allows public read access to courses and modules and nothing else. The server routes are used for actions that need the server, such as sign-in. Which of the two paths each action uses should be stated in the final report (Section 9, item 3).

## **6.2 Step 1: The Data Exists in the Database (Figure 3)**

The Supabase SQL Editor in Figure 3 runs a query that lists the first 10 modules ordered by course and position. It returns 10 rows, all of course 45fdfae1-..., with titles that read like a real syllabus.

![Figure 3][img3]

*Figure 3: Supabase SQL Editor: SELECT id, course_id, title, position FROM public.modules ORDER BY course_id, position ASC LIMIT 10 returns 10 rows.*

| **Position** | **Module title (Figure 3)** |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Module 01: Introduction to DBMS & File Systems |
| 2 | Module 02: Three-Schema Architecture |
| 3 | Module 03: Relational Model Concepts |
| 4 | Module 04: Entity-Relationship (ER) Modeling |
| 5 | Module 05: Enhanced ER (EER) Modeling |
| 6 | Module 06: Relational Algebra Operations |
| 7 | Module 07: SQL DDL Statements |
| 8 to 10 | Further modules (the next rows continue with SQL DML and later topics; partly cut off in the screenshot) |

- **Each row has an `id`, a `course_id`, a `title` and a `position`:** the structure designed in Week 4 (Module entity: course link, title, content, order).

- **Positions run 1, 2, 3...:** the order that the reader displays (rule BR-01).

- **The course ids are UUIDs,** as in the Week 4 schema, and match the address format of the course page (/course/4639bd3d-...).

- **The query was written and run by hand in the dashboard.** This is a good verification step to keep: whenever the screen looks wrong, run the same query to see whether the problem is in the data or in the code.

**Good design points visible in Figure 5**

The layout is clean and focused on reading: a fixed module list beside a wide reading card; headings and lists render correctly; the two actions that matter (summary and quiz) are visible without scrolling; the open-access rule of the SRS is respected because the page shows no login wall.

## **6.5 End-to-End Proof**

| **Stage** | **Proof** | **Figure** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data stored | The modules table holds ordered modules; courses holds 3 courses. | 3, 4 |
| Read by the server / client | The administrator list and the dashboard totals match the stored data (3 and 21). | 2, 4 |
| Shown in the interface | The same course appears in the reader with its 21 modules and Markdown content. | 5 |
| Written from the interface | Courses that were absent in Week 5 are now present, created through the form or the database. | 4 |
| Same data in every place | Dashboard (21 modules) equals the reader list (21) for SE-01; Total Courses (3) equals the list in Figure 4. | 2, 4, 5 |

**To complete the proof**

Capture one round trip in a single sequence: create a new course in the form, see the row appear, then find the same row in the Supabase courses table, and finally delete it and confirm that it disappears from both places. This closes the loop for writes.

# **8. Git and Housekeeping**

## **8.1 Pending Changes**

The Source Control badge shows 9 changed files and the status bar shows main*: the work of the week is sitting uncommitted on the main branch (Figures 1 and 2).

| **Marker** | **Files seen in the explorer** | **Meaning** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| U (untracked, new) | app/api/auth/login/route.ts, app/api/notes/route.ts, lib/supabaseAdmin | New files that Git does not know yet. |
| M (modified) | app/course/[id]/page.tsx, app/login/page.tsx, package.json, package-lock.json | Existing files that were changed. |
| Others | app/auth/callback (new folder) and further files making up the count of 9 | Check the Source Control list for the complete set. |

## **8.2 Branch Workflow**

Week 5 protected main, so a direct push of these changes will be refused. Use the workflow from the Week 5 report: create a feature branch, commit in small steps, push the branch and open a pull request. Splitting the changes into separate commits also makes the history readable:

| **Suggested commit** | **Contains** |
| --- | --- |
| feat(auth): add login route and auth callback | app/api/auth/login/route.ts, app/auth/callback, app/login/page.tsx |
| feat(api): add notes route | app/api/notes/route.ts, lib/supabaseAdmin |
| feat(course): render module content with Markdown | app/course/[id]/page.tsx |
| chore(deps): add react-markdown | package.json, package-lock.json |

**Check before committing**

The explorer shows a .env file in the project (Figure 2). Make sure it is still ignored by Git and that the new server-side file lib/supabaseAdmin does not contain a key written directly in the code. Secrets belong in .env only.

## **8.3 Dependency Audit**

Figure 1 reports 5 high-severity vulnerabilities and offers npm audit fix --force. The forced fix can upgrade packages to incompatible versions and break the project, so use it only as a last step.

- Run npm audit to see the list: which packages, how serious and whether a fix exists.

- Check whether each package is used at run time or only for development tools; development-only problems matter less for the deployed site.

- Run npm audit fix without --force first; it applies safe updates only.

- For what remains, update the direct package that pulls in the problem, or note it as an accepted risk with the reason.

- Run npm run build after any update and capture the result.

# **10. Risks and Next Steps**

## **10.1 Risks**

| **Risk** | **Impact** | **Mitigation** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calculations are written inside page components | Hard to test, easy to make inconsistent between screens | Move them to one domain module with tests (Section 4.6). |
| A server key ends up in browser code or in Git | Full access to the database | Only NEXT_PUBLIC_ values in the browser; .env ignored; review lib/supabaseAdmin. |
| Public read access is wider than intended | Private data visible to visitors | Row Level Security policies per table (Week 5, Section 6.6). |
| Unvalidated input reaches the database | Bad data, crashes or injection | Server-side validation and database constraints (Section 5). |
| Changes stay uncommitted on main | Lost work, rejected push | Feature branch and pull request (Section 8). |
| Unresolved development issue and audit findings | Instability and security debt | Sections 5.6 and 8.3. |

## **10.2 Known Limitations**

- Only the Dashboard and Courses tabs of the administrator area are shown working; Modules and MCQ Banks are still to be demonstrated.

- The quiz bank is empty (0 MCQs), so quiz scoring cannot be shown yet.

- The AI summary result is not shown in the screenshots.

- The reader displays progress, but the action that changes it is not shown.

# **Appendix A: Glossary**

| **Term** | **Meaning** |
| --- | --- |
| Business logic | The rules and calculations that belong to the product itself, such as progress and quiz score. |
| Domain module | One place in the code that holds the business logic as plain functions, separate from screens and database calls. |
| Vertical slice | One feature built through all layers: interface, server and database. |
| Server-side validation | Checking input on the server, which cannot be bypassed, in addition to checks in the browser. |
| Error code | A short stable word such as VALIDATION_ERROR that screens can react to, in addition to the HTTP status number. |
| Route handler | A Next.js file (route.ts) that answers requests to an address such as /api/notes. |
| Dynamic route | A page whose address contains a variable part, such as /course/<id>. |
| Markdown | A simple text format with symbols for headings, lists and bold text; rendered into formatted text by react-markdown. |
| Row Level Security (RLS) | Database rules that decide which rows each caller may read or write. |
| npm audit | A command that checks installed packages against a list of known security problems. |
| Untracked / modified (U / M) | VS Code markers: a new file that Git does not track yet / a tracked file with changes. |
